Surprisingly one of my favorite games. It is really satisfying to hack computers and it is as dramatic as it can be without getting too unrealistic. One of my favorite details in the game is that you can choose to use mainly the gui OR you can use mainly the terminal. It has many action packed parts despite the fact that you are just staring at a virtual screen. One of the tensest moments I can remember ever experiencing in a videogame was in the DLC of Hacknet. For this sort of game, the story almost doesn't matter, but it has a pretty good story as well. It really makes you feel powerful, unstoppable, and... well... like a hacker.

While Hacknet is good game by itself, having previously played Uplink, a game which Hacknet seems to heavily borrow from, I feel it is hard not to compare the two. The core game play loop of Hacknet seems to be very similar to that of Uplink, being that it boils down to:

1.) Get a hacking mission
2.) Survey and prepare any prerequisites needed for this specific target
3.) Start your hack and watch some progress bars
4.) Do whatever the mission specified
5.) Cover your tracks and leave.

And while I believe that Hacknet does a perfectly fine job of implementing this gameplay loop effectively, it feels to me as if it's just a stripped down version of Uplink. I am in no way trying to say that Hacknet is a bad game, however when comparing things like depth and variety of hacking programs, network map, and overall story progression, it's hard not to see it as an overall regression from what came before.

Overall, I'd say that Hacknet's strong suit when compared to Uplink is it's gui. While Uplink's clunky design really hasn't aged all that well, Hacknet's gui makes playing through missions feel that much smoother. On top of this, one of the most prominent features that distinguishes Hacknet from Uplink, is that Hacknet's gameplay centers more around executing terminal commands, meaning that very few operations need to be completed with a mouse. This has the rather enjoyable side effect of really making it feel like your hacking, as frantically typing in commands during a hack closely emulates what you might expect to see a hacker do on TV or in a movie.

If you haven't played Uplink, give it a try with the UplinkOS mod first, but if you've already tried it, Hacknet is a decent successor that's worth playing.

[h1]A Hacking Simulator Unlike Any Other [/h1]
Hacknet is an amazing game with fantastic immersiveness. I'd usually sit down to play for 20 minutes, but get lost for hours... There are several things I liked about this game:
[list]
[*] The degree to which the game is close to console controlled system manipulations
[*] Content which can be found all across the network of PCs. (the logs and notes)
[*] The branching storyline
[*] The amazing and varying soundtrack
[/list]
Overall, my experience with this game was quite good. I enjoyed the storyline and liked the control the creators gave me over any computer in the game. I'd recommend this game to anyone who likes puzzles and typing (as this game is basically typing A LOT).

Hacknet isn't a perfect simulation of real system administration or network security concepts (such as how it thinks "ports" and "shells" work), but it gets close enough that after an initial learning curve, the difference between Hacknet and reality isn't distracting.  The high-level goals make sense in the context of freelance network intrusion, and the routine gameplay mechanics of scanning log files and running canned utilities/scripts are pretty true-to-life.

It's also really fun, with just enough time-sensitive gameplay (trace evasion) to keep things tense, and plenty of mysteries to uncover as you explore a target's filesystem.

Definitely the best text-based "hacking" game I've played yet.
